results.dimension1_explanation: The AI fundamentally misidentified the cone's apex. It assumed L (the vertex on line EF) was the apex and K, M (on line CD) were base-circle points, leading to an impossible contradiction (Q cannot be the midpoint of KM if Q is on the z-axis and K,M are on a side of the square). The standard solution reveals that M is the apex and K, L are the base-circle points (with KL as the diameter), which resolves all geometric contradictions.
results.dimension2_explanation: The standard solution uses 3D coordinate geometry and the Pythagorean theorem: it identifies the correct apex (M on line CD), computes KL=14 as the diameter (giving radius R=7), then uses the right triangle MQP (where QP⊥CD, QP=√13) with MQ²+QP²=MK²=196 to find the height h=√183. This is a spatial geometry technique, not modular arithmetic.
results.ai_direction_summary: The AI set up coordinates correctly but assumed L (on EF) was the cone's apex and K, M (on CD) were base points, then spent the entire thinking process trapped in an irreconcilable contradiction about Q being the midpoint of KM.
results.standard_solution_key_technique: The standard solution correctly identifies M (on CD) as the apex and K, L as base-circle diameter endpoints, then applies the 3D Pythagorean theorem in right triangle MQP to compute the cone's height.

results.dimension1_explanation: The AI correctly identified the problem as chip-firing/abelian sandpile on a 3-regular tree and recognized the abelian property (the key starting point of the standard solution), and even correctly computed small cases (n=1,3,4,9 work). However, the AI missed the crucial turning point: exploiting the symmetry that all cities at the same distance from the capital have the same number of tourists, reducing the problem to a 1D sequence c_n = (a_0, a_1, a_2, ...). Instead, the AI went down a complex recursive rabbit hole defining B(k) and F(k) functions for binary subtrees and computing values case-by-case, never converging to the clean pattern n = 3·2^k - 2 or 3·2^k - 3.

results.ai_direction_summary: The AI correctly identified the abelian sandpile framework but took a wrong turn into complex recursive B(k)/F(k) subtree analysis without exploiting the radial symmetry that reduces the problem to one dimension.
